opus-5.5.text:
I think it depends a lot on why you're learning the skill in the first place. If the only reason is that you expect to sell it in the labor market, then yes, the case gets weaker once a model can do it better and more cheaply than you. But that's rarely the whole story.

One point is that being outperformed on a benchmark isn't the same as being replaceable in practice. Models are often very good at well-specified, self-contained tasks, but a lot of real work involves knowing which problem to solve, catching when something has gone subtly wrong, and integrating results into a larger context. If you don't understand a domain yourself, you can't really evaluate what the model gives you. So learning the skill is partly about becoming a competent supervisor or collaborator, and that remains valuable even when you're not the one doing the bulk of the execution.

Another point is that skills compound in ways that are hard to foresee. Learning mathematics, for example, doesn't just teach you to prove theorems. It changes how you reason about everything else. Even if a model can prove the theorems faster, the cognitive habits you build are still yours, and they shape how well you can think about questions the models aren't yet being pointed at.

And then there's the plain consumption value. People still play chess even though engines have been far better than any human for decades. Chess is arguably more popular now than ever. A lot of people learn things because they find them intrinsically rewarding, and AI doesn't really take that away.

That said, I'd be honest that if AI keeps improving the way I expect, the economic return to many skills will fall over time. I don't think people should pretend otherwise. My rough heuristic is: learn things you find interesting, learn things that help you understand and steer the tools you're using, and be somewhat skeptical of investing years in a narrow skill whose only value is that it's currently scarce, because that scarcity may not last.

r001.rationale: The response says skills can compound and that mathematics can change how someone reasons about other questions, but it does not clearly identify complementarity with that person’s other skills as the reason the skill remains valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's useful to separate two different reasons you might learn a skill. One is instrumental: you want the output the skill produces. The other is that the skill changes how you think, what you can notice, and what you can evaluate.

On the first one, I think the honest answer is that a lot of the instrumental value does go away. If a model can write the code or do the translation better and cheaper than I can, then learning it purely to produce that output is a bad trade, in the same way that learning to do long division by hand quickly is a bad trade today. People sometimes resist that conclusion, but I don't think it's really controversial once you say it plainly.

But the second category is more robust than people assume, at least for now. If you can't do something at all, you often can't tell whether the model did it well. You can't ask good questions, you can't spot when it's confidently wrong, and you can't decompose a problem in a way that lets you delegate pieces of it. A lot of what I actually do with models today depends on having enough of the underlying skill to supervise them. So the skill becomes less about execution and more about judgment, and judgment is still scarce.

There's also a selection effect in which skills you keep. Something like chess is the extreme case: engines have been better than any human for decades, and people still learn chess because the point was never the output. For most work skills, that's not the situation, so you have to be honest with yourself about which bucket you're in.

The caveat I'd add is that this is a transitional argument. If models get good enough that you can trust them without being able to check them, which is what we'd expect if capabilities keep improving, then the supervisory value erodes too. At that point the remaining reasons to learn things look more like the chess case: you do it because you find it interesting or because it's part of being a competent person, not because the economy rewards it. I don't think we're there yet, but I'd be planning as if it's a few years away rather than a few decades.

r001.rationale: The response says that knowing the underlying skill helps someone ask better questions, spot errors, decompose problems, and supervise AI—ways the skill complements their ability to use models effectively.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you want the skill for. If you enjoy doing something, the fact that an AI can do it better doesn't seem like a strong reason to stop. People still play chess even though computers are much better than any human.

If you're learning a skill for its economic value, then you do have to take AI capabilities into account. But I wouldn't equate “the model is better than me at this” with “there's no value in understanding it.” Knowing something about programming, for example, can help you decide what to ask for and judge whether the result actually solves your problem, even if the model writes better code than you do.

The harder question is how long that advantage lasts. If models become good enough to make those judgments as well, then the economic case for learning the skill could weaken further. So I'd distinguish between learning because you want to understand or enjoy something, and learning as an investment in your future earning potential. AI changes the second calculation much more directly than the first.

r001.rationale: The candidate says understanding programming can help someone prompt and evaluate AI output, but does not identify complementarity with the person’s other skills as a reason the skill remains valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on why you’re learning the skill. If you’re learning it because you enjoy it, the fact that an AI can do it better doesn’t seem especially relevant. People still play chess even though computers are much better than any human.

If you’re learning it for its economic value, then you have to think about what the skill will allow you to do in combination with AI. A model being better than you at some task doesn’t necessarily mean that learning about that task is useless. You might still need enough understanding to ask useful questions, evaluate the answers, and figure out how they fit into what you’re trying to accomplish.

But I also wouldn’t assume that those roles will remain valuable forever. If AI gets better at evaluating its own work and deciding what to do, that argument becomes weaker. So I think there’s a real distinction between learning something because you find it worthwhile and learning it as an investment in future earnings. The second is becoming more uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response says a skill may help in combination with AI and help someone ask questions, evaluate answers, and pursue goals. It does not clearly identify complementarity with the person’s other skills as the reason the skill remains valuable.
